title: Rubato: Transcribing Piano Music with Timestamps
claim: A structured text representation can losslessly serialize polyphonic notation and timing into a single readable sequence for sequence-to-sequence models.
layout: Score on top-left, piano roll below, token string bottom-left, narration right
description: The figure shows how a two-bar piano excerpt is converted into the InterMo text representation. At top left is a engraved grand-staff score in 3/4 with four flats. Below it is a piano-roll view with orange note dots and lines for the upper staff, teal ones for the lower staff, and gray and black bars marking metric intervals. A small legend labels 'Intervals' and 'Moments'. Beneath this, the InterMo token sequence is printed as color-coded chips: black for bar and key markers, gray for durations, orange and teal for right-hand and left-hand staff markers and pitches. On the right, a stack of boxed rows gives an English narration of each token group, such as 'Wait a quarter note' and 'Release c5, press D-5'. The color coding links all three views, so the eye follows the score to the roll to the tokens to the narration.
caption: \textbf{\intermo{} representation.} Left, top to bottom: A two-bar piano excerpt, decomposed into metric intervals (gray/black) and pitched moments (orange = upper staff, teal = lower staff), serialized as a 1D text sequence. Right: English narration of \intermo{}, segmented into interval-piece pretokenization borders which follow a canonical order within score moments ([ref]). Uppercase = onset, lowercase = offset; \# = sharp, - = flat (e.g., \prpitch{A-3}: A$\flat$3). Staff markers (\pr{}\pl{}, for piano right and left hands, respectively) emitted only on change.
abstract: We consider the conversion of musical recordings into human-readable sheet music annotated with timestamps. Such output lets a listener clearly visualize rubato (temporally expressive playing), a learner diagnose ensemble precision and timing choices against the written music, and a musicology scholar compare performance styles across recordings of the same work. We introduce (1) a prompt-conditioned encoder-decoder model, named Rubato, trained to output (2) a new textual representation for polyphonic music, named InterMo, which we designed for compatibility with sequence-to-sequence training. Our experiments demonstrate that Rubato produces timestamped piano sheet music from audio with higher notational accuracy than the best existing approaches, which are based on cascades. We find that even if the cascade is given ground-truth MIDI instead of audio, Rubato performs better, suggesting that the ceiling of existing approaches is primarily representational, not acoustic. Further, because Rubato is trained on several related tasks (with prompts), it competes with or outperforms the best single-task systems on related but simpler tasks like MIDI note grounding and beat/downbeat detection. A demo is available at https://nctamer.github.io/rubato-transcription .
